# Hard-to-vary report: the Time Traveller's argument for time travel

## 1. The question, frozen

The opening scene makes one explanation central: the Time Traveller's case for why movement through Time should be possible, just as movement through Space is. What is asked: does his chain of reasoning (four dimensions, consciousness's one-way drift, the gravity/balloon analogy, the vanishing model) actually establish that conclusion, over the range of this one dinner-party argument plus its "experimental verification"? This is an **argument** (a case for a conclusion), not a diagnosis or a story-craft question, because the text presents it as reasoned steps meant to convince named sceptics (Filby, the Medical Man, the Psychologist).

## 2. The explanation in parts

- **P1 — Duration is a dimension.** No real cube can lack duration; therefore any real thing has Length, Breadth, Thickness, *and* Duration.
- **P2 — The apparent difference is only in us.** Time seems unlike Space only because "our consciousness moves along it" one way, at one rate.
- **P3 — The gravity analogy.** We once had no free vertical movement; balloons gave it to us. By parity, we may yet learn to alter our rate or direction along Time.
- **P4 — We already partly move in time.** Vivid recollection is "jumping back" a little.
- **P5 — The demonstration.** The model vanishes when the lever is pressed; offered as experimental verification of P1–P4.
- **P6 — The visibility patch.** When asked why a machine gone to the *past* wasn't visible last Thursday, the Psychologist supplies "presentation below the threshold... diluted presentation": moving fast through time makes a thing proportionately fainter.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P1 (duration is a dimension) | **Borrowed** | Rests on a geometrical convention (a "real" thing needs extension) that is itself asserted, not tested here; the argument imports it from outside and never pokes it. |
| P2 (difference is only in consciousness) | **Loose** | Swap it for "the difference is that space is reversible and time is not" and the rest of the speech (balloons, drift) reads almost the same. Nothing in the change list distinguishes the two claims. |
| P3 (gravity/balloon analogy) | **Loose** | Swap the analogy for "we once thought sound couldn't be captured, then came the phonograph" — the rhetorical force is identical. What's actually held is the weak, general point that present limits aren't proof of permanent limits, which supports "maybe" and nothing stronger. |
| P4 (memory as mini time-travel) | **Idle** | Remove it and the argument's conclusion is unaffected; it is offered as a softening intuition pump, not a load-bearing step. |
| P5 (the vanishing) | **Held if** | It is held only by the added job "rule out a mundane trick," and that job is exactly what the text leaves untested at this point — Filby and the narrator both flag "trickery" and "conjuror," and nothing in the scene distinguishes real time-travel from sleight of hand. So P5 is held only *if* the trick-explanation can be ruled out, which hasn't happened yet. |
| P6 (diluted presentation) | **Unknown / catch-all** | It is supplied on the spot, after an objection, with no gauge: no reading is named that would show it swallowing the failure rather than explaining it. It could equally "explain" the opposite finding (the model staying visible) by adjusting the diluting factor after the fact. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

- **Flip:** Had the model *not* vanished, would the same speech still have been given as proof? Nothing here shows it couldn't — the theory (P1–P4) is argued independently of P5's outcome, so the "verification" is decorative until an outcome is committed to in advance, which the text never does within this excerpt.
- **Direction/reverse:** The vanishing is read as evidence *for* the theory (identification from evidence), not as something the theory *predicts and nothing else could* (production). A rival cause — a hidden mechanism, a puff of misdirection — produces the identical vanishing. At this point in the story the two are, by the method's own rule, **the same explanation at this level**: no change on the list (only "watch the table") tells them apart.
- **Answer hidden in the starting points:** P2 already assumes what P3–P5 are meant to prove — that time is space-like enough to be travelled — by calling the difference a mere fact "about consciousness." That is close to circular: the conclusion is smuggled into the description of the premise.
- **Where jobs came from:** The job "must survive Filby's and the Medical Man's scepticism" is given (the text stages it explicitly). The job "must rule out conjuring" is one I added; the text itself gestures at it (Filby's "sleight-of-hand," the narrator's "no trickery" insistence) but never resolves it inside this excerpt.
- **Catch-alls and gauges:** P6 is a catch-all with no gauge, exactly as flagged above.
- **What the change list leaves out, openly or not:** The argument never states what change would falsify it (what would count as *not* time travel), so its own boundary is undeclared rather than honestly narrowed.
- **Where parts came from:** P1 and P2 are asserted; P3 is built (a constructed analogy) but tested against no counter-case; P5 is seen (witnessed) but its interpretation is asserted, not built.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

Two changes would tighten it most: (a) naming, before the demonstration, some outcome the theory forbids and a conjuring trick would allow (or vice versa), so P5 stops being "held if" and becomes properly tested; (b) giving P6 a gauge — some feature of the vanishing (a residue, a measurable delay, a return) that a mere trick could not also produce. Notably, the later chapters do supply exactly this: the full-size machine, the Time Traveller's own bodily wear (dust, wounds) on return, and eight days of internally consistent detail are new jobs that a stage trick cannot cheaply satisfy. Those add real weight — but they lie outside this excerpt's argument as given.

## 6. What this does not show

None of this shows the four-dimension theory is false, or that no time machine could work — a false idea can still be argued this loosely, and a sound idea can be argued this loosely too. It only shows which parts of *this particular speech* are doing work (the demonstration, held conditionally) and which are decoration or unearned (the consciousness gloss, the balloon analogy, the on-the-spot patch). As fiction, several of these — the choice of a balloon rather than another analogy, the choice to have the Psychologist rather than Filby supply the patch — may also be free narrative choices rather than claims needing to be "explained" at all; that is a separate, story-craft question this report has not tried to answer.

## 7. One next step

Reread Chapters III–VI (already partly in this excerpt) as an **added job** test: does the Time Traveller's own return — his wounds, hunger, torn socks, eight subjective days — do work that the party-trick rival cannot also do cheaply? If so, that is where the explanation actually starts to earn its keep; the opening argument alone does not.
